title: Buddhist Practice for Climate Change
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The talk's main teaching is that Buddhist principles can guide us in responding to climate change by cultivating individual actions of compassion and wisdom, while also acknowledging the importance of collective action and systemic change. Shuko Edie Norton encourages listeners to reflect on their own role in addressing climate change and to find ways to integrate their Buddhist practice with taking action in the world. By starting small and being mindful of our intentions, we can make a positive impact, even if it feels overwhelming or uncertain, and by supporting efforts like lawsuits against oil companies, we can work towards a common goal of protecting the environment.

sentences.text: **Shuko Edie Norton:** Good evening.
Thank you for being here.
This month we're doing dharma talks on old koans, the paradoxical stories that are meant to enlighten us suddenly.
My talk this evening is about a contemporary koan, climate change.
This is a very challenging topic that we are just learning to come to terms with.
As far as I know, there were no ancient koans about climate change, so I made up a couple.
What is the sound of climate change?
And does a category five hurricane have Buddha nature?
So I'm actually going to be reporting on an online course that four of us in the sangha took over the last couple of months.
It was put on by One Earth Sangha, a Buddhist environmentalist online organization.
They had a similar course in 2015, and this is the second year they've had it.
It was about Buddhist practice for the enormous problem of climate change.
The sessions provided inspiration, information, and reflection on how to use our Buddhist practice, our ecological bodhisattva practice.
That's what the word means, eco-sattva: to work together to reduce the impact of climate change on our earth.
At this point, it's believed that we won't be able to stop climate change, but we could reduce the impact of it, and there are many things we can do collectively and individually to do this.
I want to share some of the material from the course.
It was quite a rich course, so I can't share it all, but some major points that I hope will be useful to you.

Looking at climate change, the increasingly devastating storms, fires, floods, droughts, and the wars and dislocations and political, social, and economic upheavals going on in the world, we see that individual actions are not enough to stem this tide.
We must work together to change systemic causes of climate change, such as the growth imperative of capitalism, requiring ever more natural resources;

consumerism, always craving, always getting more stuff; extractivism, believing there is always more we can take out of the earth without penalty; unregulated and subsidized corporate behavior, polluting air and water, using up resources for which we taxpayers pay; politics increasingly controlled by corporate interests, not community needs and values.
So how do we respond to these current contemporary conditions?
What to do?
Buddhist principles can guide us to actions we can take.
First of all, abstain from all evil.
In practical terms, that may mean we can rescind subsidies to fossil fuel corporations.
Apparently there are $37.5 billion annually spent on subsidies to corporations through various mechanisms.
We can impose a carbon tax to ensure economic justice, not taxpayer-supported.
We can reject pipelines and infrastructure that support fossil fuel extraction, and we know about those in the Northwest and in North Dakota and South Dakota.
We can prohibit fuel transportation that pollutes and endangers communities, and we're worried about the oil trains going through here.
We can reject trade agreements like the TPP, the Trans-Pacific Partnership, that give global corporations economic control over local needs and values.
We can shift from meat agriculture in order to reduce dependence on grain and the cruelty to the animals involved in meat production.
So: abstain from all evil, and cultivate all good.
Subsidize clean renewable energy, individually and governmentally.
Refurbish old buildings rather than using up irreplaceable resources to build new ones.
Create more and better public transit to cut fossil fuel use.
Establish more ecological agricultural models and climate-friendly diets, that is, no meat.
And we can also purify our own minds.
Develop contentment to replace consumerism.
Focus on spiritual values, qualitative growth rather than quantitative acquisition.
Develop wisdom, understand the consequences of our actions.
Arouse compassion in ourselves for all people, no exclusions.
Advocate justice for all, no bigotry, racism, sexism, et cetera.
These are all earth-friendly behaviors that we can take up.
And finally, we can benefit all beings.
We can vote.
I'm sure we did this election.
We'll have to do it again.
Petition elected officials.
Invest money from fossil fuel companies.
Invest in environmental-friendly ones.
The Buddhist teaching that suffering is caused by greed, hate, and ignorance or delusion helps us to understand that these actions and changes are needed if we are to save the earth.
Joanna Macy, widely known for her long work in deep ecology, advises as follows, quote:
*Our individualistic destructive culture discounts our deep concern for the earth, our home.
When we think about the enormity of the problem of climate change, we usually react in one of two ways.
We feel helpless, overwhelmed, and we shut down.
Or in our panic and grief about what's happening, we look for someone to blame, and then we shut down.
How can we keep from these two ineffective reactions?*
*We can take refuge in sangha.
We can help each other.
We in sangha remind each other that our practice asks us to face the present moment, whatever its contents.
We look to each other to help us speak without defensiveness.
We trust each other to speak truthfully about ourselves and our feelings.
We speak about our love of the earth as well as our fears for it and for ourselves.
In effect, we practice our true relationship, which is interdependent, interbeing.* She ends this recommendation with:
*To do what the earth needs now, we need to shift from our current individually oriented, care less orientation to acknowledging the true situation, which requires radical change.
And we need to support each other in this effort, and we can.*
The EcoSatva course sessions offered questions to participants to answer as it went along, and there was some back and forth from participants to the main video and audio portion of the course.
Actually, I think about 1,100 people around the world took this course this year.
You might want to answer these questions and, if possible, discuss them with a friend.
I've asked Thales to include a written copy of this talk so that you can look at these questions and maybe think about them.
They were thought provoking and got us engaged in what the issues are and how we might respond to them.
There are eight of them.
The first one is: when I see what is happening in our world, to our world, what breaks my heart is, and then you fill in the blank.
So it's reflecting on your own panic, sorrow, bewilderment.
It asks you also to notice your physical sensations when you're thinking about this, including numbing or shutting down.
Get in touch with our bodies about this problem.
Number two: to what extent do I invest in my Buddhist practice as an escape?
Can I integrate my zazen practice with engaging in the world, taking action on climate change, in other words?
Three: what is the balance between my propensity toward reflection and toward action?
Do I want to change this balance?
In what ways would I change it?
Four: what prevents me from closer collaboration with others on this issue?
How might I overcome these obstacles?
Five: are there places in my life where I can sense a new perspective that might help me make change?
Six: how do I hold on to my habitual behaviors about taking action?
Where do I see I could take a spiritual risk?
For instance, does not knowing if I will succeed prevent me from acting?
Can I practice not knowing and still engage anyway?
Seven: what would stretch me as an eco-sattva, one who saves the earth?
What arises in my body when I imagine doing or being this?
And eight: what does my heart tell me will support my continued eco-sattva journey toward saving the earth?
So climate change is a really big challenge.
We don't know if we can be successful in reducing its effects, but I believe we must try for the sake of our children and future generations.
I believe it has fallen to us, those of us alive and walking around and generally healthy, to make our best effort to reduce the harm to our planet that has begun to manifest.
But what can we as individuals do that will have any substantial impact on such an enormous problem?
It's easy to feel helpless and to return to being numb.

We can reduce our personal use of fossil fuels, things that most of us already do, like taking public transportation or riding bikes or walking, turning off our lights, using energy-saving light bulbs and appliances, installing solar energy, et cetera.
These are all good, but not enough for this big problem.

There are political actions that must be taken as well: letter writing, calling Congress and state representatives, educating ourselves, going to meetings, supporting petitions, speaking at city council meetings, attending rallies, going on marches, et cetera.
But what if we don't have the time or the information or even the inclination to do these pro-political things?
How do we find something to do that could help even a little bit?
I have thought about this for myself because of my age.
I can't go marching anymore.
I have some physical limitations.
So here's what I have done to figure out what to do, and what I offer to you as a suggestion.
First, reflect on what your heart tells you you'd like to do, what action you are drawn to.
Second, think about the ways in which you might implement that action.
Think small, not big.
Think small, what you can do pretty easily because you already know how to do it.
For instance, are you hesitant to reveal how scared or overwhelmed you feel about this subject?
Then ask a trusted friend to have a conversation with you about it.
Talking will help, and it might even lead to some action you could take.
Are you curious or worried about what friends or coworkers think or know about climate change?
Ask them, what do you think about climate change?
Or, do you think the recent flood or hurricane or drought or whatever was caused by climate change?
You don't have to engage in an argument with the person, but you can raise awareness by just asking the question.
And I think awareness is the first thing we have to do: get many people aware.
Are you drawn to speaking at a meeting but you don't know enough to do so?
Make your first action educating yourself about your topic.
There's a lot online.
After that, figure out what meetings to go to, and go and start talking.
Do you regularly communicate by Facebook or read or respond to a blog?
Try posting your response or do a new post as a way of taking action and getting other people to be aware.
Do you like to write?
Study a concern and write an email to your congress senator or representative, or to the editor of the paper.
You can do this online through the congress addresses, or you can certainly write to a local or far away paper.
Are you better on the phone than on email?
Prepare a statement and call your congressman or senator and talk with one of his or her assistants about your concern.
I've always been really afraid of calling Congress.
There's too much authority there.
So I decided this is one thing I'm going to learn how to do, and I did it this past week.

I called the Department of Justice of the United States, the attorney general of all things, and spoke into a recorder, which was easier for me to do, and this was not about climate change but about the electoral college.
But that's the thing I'm going to do: call now.
Are you good at creating posters or signs or artwork?
Prepare visuals for meetings or marches or handouts to distribute.
If you're good at computer stuff and you know a group that needs some help in organizing things on the computer,
offer your services for that.
There are many, many ways that we can each use our current skills to get involved a little bit and develop new skills to keep us going.
This type of self-reflection, of course, is good for more than just the issue of climate change.
There are lots of other issues going on now and there will be in the new administration.
Health care: the repeal of the Affordable Care Act is going to be a big topic.
Safeguarding democratic processes for the press, for public and public roles.
Women's issues, misogyny, reproductive rights, rights of diverse identities, racial minorities, LGBT, religious groups, immigrants.
There are many, many things that we can pay attention to and need to at this point.
So reflect on what you want for yourself, what draws you, what your heart tells you.
Then act, and then come for refuge and support in the sangha.
In the final sessions of the EcoSatva course, they emphasized coming together in sangha for moral support and for our teachings.
Also getting past demonizing the other, instead realizing that we, everyone on earth, are all in this together.
So we must include those with whom we disagree.
The course ended by offering the following Buddhist principles to guide us in our effort.
First of all, realize everything is sacred.
Second, listen deferentially to others in order to really hear what others are saying.
Compassion is a third thing.
Forgiving mistakes, our own and others'.
Honesty with self and others.
Generosity.
Humility, not pushing our agenda as the only way.
And finally wisdom, honoring the wisdom in all of us.
This quote was not in the course, I don't think, but it's a good one to end on.
Wendell Berry, who is an American environmentalist and poet and farmer, had the following encouraging words for these days:
*Be joyful even though you have considered the facts.*
I have a handout to give you too.
If you would like it, I'll put it out on the counter in the lobby.
It's short answers to hard questions about climate change.
It's actually six pages of these.
It's by the New York Times last year, in 2015.
And it asks questions like, and answers them, how much is the planet heating up?
How much trouble are we in?
What's an optimistic scenario?
Reducing meat in my diet to help the climate, et cetera.
So that's very interesting.
I made copies of that.
And I'd be happy to encourage you to speak, a few minutes, ten minutes, if you have questions or comments.
**Participant:** I have a question.
Are you aware of any groups in Bellingham that are meeting to talk about climate change and what to do about it?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I think the 350.org, which is Bill McKibben's group, which is a national organization, I think that is forming something here.
And I haven't heard specifically about people yet.
But I don't know of any other group at this point.
Does anyone else know about it?
**Participant:** There was a group, there was a whole sort of movement a little bit earlier called Transition to a Post.
It was national, but there were local groups too.
Is that still active?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I don't know.
But the Restore certainly works on those issues.
I think this online group, One Earth Sangha, intends to continue and be a resource to people.
But I do think it helps to have real life companions in this.
The little group of us met several times during the period of this course to talk about things, and that grounded it, it made it more real.
And Resources, which is the parent group that has the Restore, they're quite active in some very specific legal ways.
Like they're currently suing Burlington Northern to get them to cover the coal trains, because quite a bit of coal dust is released over the 1,000 mile journey from Montana.
And that's some victories, actually.
I think pretty effective.
So initially it would be a good group to connect with, Resources.

I'm definitely open to anybody from our sangha, or who wants to join us in sangha, to form an alliance, especially to think about how to use Buddhist principles, particularly around people that we disagree with.
That's a really hard thing, and this is a very emotional issue, because it's the fate of the earth, I think.
And it looks like there might be a lot of opposition to progress with it in the new administration.
So that's challenging.
**Participant:** A lot of times, when we have a company we believe in, we frame it as an either-or type of thing, a black-and-white.
And usually that gets a lot of pushback.
Specifically, I came over talking with one of my co-workers, and he said climate change is BS, blah, blah, blah, and man cannot possibly have that kind of impact upon the planet.
And my response to that was, well, what if man may not be a part of the problem?
What if he is part of the problem?
And then you could see the guy's ears going in his head, and he said, well, that kind of makes sense.
So it's just a helpful little tool.
And there is a crack.
There is a crack in his eyes at some place.
And maybe that will germinate.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Definitely, in this course, they said the biggest thing we have to do is listen and help to open the topic so that people can talk about it.
**Participant:** My other religion is science.
And the Union of Concerned Scientists is a very good resource for this.
And they spend a great deal of time, in fact, they're actually currently being sued by the fossil fuel industry because they are going after them in the same way that they tobacco eventually.

I think on the documents that show that the climate science has been suppressed by the oil companies in order to hide it the same way that the information on cancer was suppressed by the tobacco in there.
And they are now being the subject of a witch hunt from the oil companies' allies in Congress.
They are going at this as an attempt to bring anti-trust legislation and so on against the oil companies.
Another very important and very good group, if you want to throw a wrench into the system, use an attorney.
And the Natural Resources Defense Council is a group of lawyers who sue everything.
They basically grind everything to a halt with legal actions.
And they are quite effective in trying to protect the environment.
It's nice to be involved at a local level, but if you have a few extra bucks and throw it at the NRDC, they will sue the government and stop them.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** What's the name again?
**Participant:** Natural Resources Defense Council, NRDC.
It is defense council in the sense of legal counsel.
So those are two groups that I would endorse.
One of the things that I think would be helpful to me is to hear about things like that going on.
That's encouraging.
I think I tend to assume everybody knows everything they know.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** So that's a great way just to have conversations and say things that we have some reason to think are probably true.
**Participant:** It's encouraging because I keep thinking somebody must be doing something, but I don't know.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Well, it keeps you going to hear that there are successes here and there.
It makes it easier to keep going against the tide.
**Participant:** I just want to say thanks for talking about it and bringing it in with our process.
I think we're all thinking about it and talking about it.
It's certainly a Buddhist teaching that we don't know what's going to happen.
So does that just mean we don't do anything?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I don't think so in this case for sure.
We don't do that in our lives anyway.
We just go ahead and do stuff.
**Participant:** Well, it is saving all these.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** It is.
But to engage and keep in mind Buddhist principles is really a good idea.
It helps to talk about it instead of just losing your temper and falling into your usual patterns.
So the sangha can be a real resource in that.
I think so.
So if anyone wants to talk with me about it, I'm really open to it.
Thank you.
**Participant:** Well, let's put on talking about it here again.
Yeah.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
